newsitem.title: USA: U.S political campaign funds controversy heats up.
newsitem.headline: U.S political campaign funds controversy heats up.

text.p: The campaign financing controversy dogging President Bill Clinton and his Democratic Party escalated on Monday, with the White House and the FBI publicly at odds over an FBI warning that China might try to funnel money into the U.S. election campaign.
Clinton on Monday said he was kept in the dark about the warning last year and is now trying to find out why.
And in an extraordinary exchange, the White House and the FBI publicly disputed the facts surrounding an FBI briefing of two intelligence specialists at the National Security Council (NSC) last June.
The White House said the FBI told the specialists of a suspected Chinese plan to "funnel money to congressional candidates", but asked the officials not to tell higher-ups.
The FBI issued a release contradicting that statement, and White House spokesman Mike McCurry immediately responded by saying the FBI statement was "in error."
China has called the charges unfounded and said on Monday it had lodged a protest with the United States.
New polls showed many Americans were concerned about the controversy, but are generally convinced the Republican Party participated in similar fund-raising practices.

ABC News and CBS News unveiled several GOP fund-raising documents on Monday, including a 1988 invitation to the White House in which fund-raisers for President Ronald Reagan urged donors to "... make your $2,500 contribution right away."

Clinton said allegations China sought to meddle in U.S. politics "would be very serious if it were true," but urged people not to jump to conclusions, saying it was important to first determine if the FBI suspicions were valid.
"Let's find out what the truth is if we can," he said.
In its statement, the FBI said it "placed no restriction whatsoever on the dissemination up the chain-of-command."
But McCurry quickly rejected that account.

"The White House legal counsel had very specific conversations with the two (White House) staffers in question. And they are adamant in recalling specifically that they were urged (by the FBI) not to disseminate the information outside the briefing room," McCurry said.
"Therefore the White House considers the FBI statement to be in error," said McCurry, who returned to the White House briefing room late on Monday to make his remarks.
Asked whether Clinton still has faith in FBI director Louis Freeh after the highly unusual public dispute, McCurry said, "Yes", but added, "I'm not going to go into it."

It is illegal for foreign governments to contribute to U.S. political campaigns. Mounting allegations that there were such efforts raise questions as to whether the objective was to buy influence over U.S. foreign and trade policy decisions.
Clinton said he was not aware of the FBI's suspicions "during the election period last year", and had he known would have asked for an investigation.

"Yes I believe I should have known. No I didn't know. If I had known, I would have asked the NSC and the chief of staff to look at the evidence and make whatever recommendations were appropriate," he told a news conference.
"This is a very serious allegation. But as far as I know, it is only that," Clinton said, adding it would be a "foolish error" for any foreign power to try to sway the outcome of a U.S. election.
Since the election, the Democratic Party has returned nearly $3 million to donors -- most with links to Asian businesses or governments -- that were deemed questionable.

Allegations of Chinese plans to interfere in U.S. politics, which first surfaced in a Washington Post report on Feb. 13, threatened to disturb a thaw in Chinese-American relations that began last year after a long estrangement.
Representative Nancy Pelosi, a California Democrat, told reporters she was warned by the FBI as early as 1991 about possible Chinese contributions to U.S. campaigns, and again last June.
McCurry said that had the administration known about the alleged Chinese effort to curry favour with U.S. leaders, it "might have acted diplomatically" to discourage this.
He said Secretary of State Madeleine Albright had raised the issue with Chinese leaders during a recent Beijing visit.

Separately, Hillary Rodham Clinton said on Monday her chief of staff Maggie Williams had acted legally in accepting a political donation at the White House but that she wished Williams had not done so "for her sake".

Mrs. Clinton also said she did not know why the Taiwanese-American entrepeneur who gave Williams the check, Johnny Chung, had visited the White House so often, but that her staff always sought to be polite to visitors.
